youtube.title: The Army Lost A War To Emus (True Story) 🦤
youtube.description:
In late 1932, about 20,000 emus moved onto the wheat farms of Western Australia, many of them run by First World War veterans. The farmers asked for help, and the Minister of Defence, Sir George Pearce, sent Major G.P.W. Meredith of the Royal Australian Artillery with two soldiers, two Lewis machine guns and 10,000 rounds.

The emus split into small groups and ran out of range. At an ambush by a dam, more than a thousand of them approached and the gun jammed. A gun mounted on a truck couldn't keep up with the birds, and the ride was too rough to aim. Army observers said each flock had a tall lookout bird that kept watch.

After about a week and 2,500 rounds, most of the emus were untouched. Parliament joked about medals and the troops were withdrawn. Meredith said the birds could "face machine guns with the invulnerability of tanks." A second attempt later that year also failed to solve the problem; in the end, bounties and fences were used instead.
